Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test asserts:
  - testMath864 sets an upper bound of 0.5 on a one-dimensional problem whose unconstrained minimum is at x = 1. It optimizes with CMAESOptimizer and asserts the returned point is within bounds (result[0] <= 0.5). The failure means the optimizer returned a value greater than 0.5.

- Reported bug summary matches the symptom:
  - “CMAESOptimizer does not enforce bounds”: Offspring can lie outside the provided bounds; default behavior does not even perform feasibility checks; and even when it does, it may accept an infeasible offspring.

- How the code allows infeasible samples to be used:
  - In doOptimize’s generation loop, offspring are generated and optionally checked for feasibility:
    - Offspring is constructed (arxk) from the current mean and random vector (xmean + ...).
    - A loop tries at most (checkFeasableCount + 1) times to get a feasible candidate, but the break condition is:
      - If i >= checkFeasableCount OR fitfun.isFeasible(...), break.
    - With checkFeasableCount at its default value 0, the condition i >= 0 is true on the first iteration, so the loop breaks immediately without ever calling isFeasible(). Thus, arxk can be infeasible and is still accepted and stored in arx.
    - Even when checkFeasableCount > 0, the loop will give up after the set number of tries and proceed with whatever arxk it has, which may still be infeasible.

- Feasibility definition and repair are decoupled from sampling:
  - FitnessFunction.isFeasible checks normalized coordinates to be between 0 and 1 when boundaries are present.
  - FitnessFunction.value uses a “repair + penalty” approach: it repairs the point into [0,1], evaluates the objective on the decoded repaired point, and adds a penalty proportional to how far the original sample was from the repaired one.
  - Critically, the sample (arx) used for selection, mean update, and later stages is not repaired before being put into the arx matrix; only the value computation uses the repaired version. Consequently, the optimizer’s internal mean and selected “best” columns can drift outside the normalized [0,1] box and remain infeasible.

- Where the returned result can become out-of-bounds:
  - The code updates the reported optimum when a better fitness is found. In the problematic implementation, because feasibility enforcement is not guaranteed in sampling, a “best” arx column can be infeasible (outside [0,1] in normalized space, hence outside [lower, upper] after decoding).
  - If the method that constructs the final returned point does not always repair-and-decode the best sample before returning (or if repair is bypassed due to configuration), the optimizer can return a decoded point that exceeds the upper bound.
  - This is consistent with the bug report: with default settings (checkFeasableCount = 0), infeasible points are accepted without any feasibility check. The fitness penalty alone does not prevent the “best” candidate from being outside bounds, especially when the true optimum lies beyond the bound (as in this test, at x = 1). The algorithm thus drifts towards that infeasible region and returns a value > 0.5.

- Why the test fails:
  - Given the unconstrained optimum is at x = 1 and there is no strict enforcement to keep offspring within bounds, the selected “best” individual and the returned point can remain outside the [lower, upper] interval. With the default configuration, the code does not guarantee repair before returning, leading to result[0] > upper[0] and the assertion failure.

In short, the generation loop’s sampling logic does not enforce feasibility by default (checkFeasableCount = 0 causes isFeasible never to be called), and even when feasibility is checked, out-of-bounds points can be accepted. Because the algorithm may not repair the selected best sample before returning, the final reported point can exceed the given bounds, exactly as observed in the failing test.
